transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-12-15 15:00 PST | Duration ~75m | Redwood: Jason Miller (AE), Priya Desai (SE), Ethan Wu (Infra) | Nimbus: Sara Patel (ML), Roberto Diaz (Infra), Mei Chen (SRE), Lucas Grant (Head AI)

Agenda: quick context, architecture constraints (on-prem/VPC), runtime tuning levers (ROPE scaling, kv-cache sharding, batching), MoE routing cost model, quantization tradeoffs, next steps and benchmarks.

Summary: deep technical session focused on how ROPE frequency/decay and token affinity affect MoE gating costs for long-context Llama/Mistral/Qwen families. Tradeoffs covered: latency vs throughput vs per-token cost, batching/kvcache strategies for on-prem NVLink vs cloud VPC, and quantization paths (PTQ / GPTQ / int8 / 4-bit). Action items and a benchmark plan agreed.

[00:00] Jason Miller: All right, hey everyone, thanks for carving out the time. Quick roll call?
[00:06] Sara Patel: Sara here, ML.
[00:08] Roberto Diaz: Roberto, infra.
[00:09] Mei Chen: Mei, SRE.
[00:10] Lucas Grant: Lucas, Head of AI.
[00:12] Priya Desai: Priya from Redwood SE.
[00:14] Ethan Wu: Ethan, infra at Redwood.
[00:15] Jason Miller: Cool. High-level objective — we want to understand the knobs for lowering MoE routing token cost while preserving latency and model quality. We'll talk ROPE tuning, kv-cache sharding, batching, and quantization.

[02:05] Sara Patel: To frame it — we have a mixture of short chat requests and longer 2k token summaries. Our infra is mostly on-prem A100 NVLink boxes but we also have a GCP region for bursts. Data residency is strict so most inference must stay in our private VPC.

[02:36] Roberto Diaz: Yes, 8xA100 per server, Mellanox EDR interconnect, and PCIe for some older racks. We're trying to estimate how much dedicated capacity to reserve vs using Redwood hosted for bursts.

[03:10] Priya Desai: Helpful. Quick callouts: MoE routing cost is primarily tokens that hit expert gates and the size of the expert states; batching and kv-cache hit-rate shape per-token GPU utilization. Also ROPE (rotary positional encodings) scaling affects attention patterns and thereby cache reuse across sequences.

[04:02] Mei Chen: Can you slow on ROPE for a sec — we've seen weird degradation on long contexts with certain models. Is this about frequency wrap or decay?

[04:10] Priya Desai: Yep, two angles. First, ROPE frequency/factor determines how quickly positional phase rotates; scaling it (we call it rope-frequency multiplier) can reduce aliasing for long distances but might shift attention patterns, reducing kv-cache locality. Second, rope decay (some teams apply a soft decay to older positions) can—intentionally—deprioritize far tokens to improve effective cache hit rate for sliding windows. Both impact whether tokens map consistently to the same gating decisions in MoE.

[05:05] Sara Patel: So if we tweak ROPE to improve long context quality, we might make routing less stable? That could cause more tokens to be routed to different experts and spike cost, right?

[05:12] Priya Desai: Exactly. We gave a simple example: with Llama-style rotary at default, repeating patterns in the prompt yield predictable gating; when you change the frequency multiplier by x1.5, the anchor points shift and some tokens that used to be 'expert local' start flopping, leading to more expert diversity and routing overhead.

[06:00] Ethan Wu: On the infra side, that means more cross-GPU transfers unless you pin experts per GPU and accept load imbalance. On NVLink meshes that's doable but on mixed PCIe racks it's painful.

[06:30] Roberto Diaz: We wanted to ask — what's Redwood's recommendation for sharding kv-cache when running MoE? We currently keep a single global kv per model instance.

[06:45] Priya Desai: For MoE with high routing entropy we recommend a hybrid: shard experts across GPUs but also split KV cache by prefix buckets. If your workload has a lot of repeated prefixes across requests, a prefix-based cache (per-tenant) helps. For more random traffic, continuous batching with per-request routing maps and a central routing table works better to avoid memory duplication.

[07:30] Lucas Grant: Are there perf numbers you can share — like latencies at 128 vs 1k tokens for Llama vs Mistral?

[07:40] Jason Miller: We ran internal benchmarks on a mixed 8xA100 NVLink box: Llama-2-13B (MoE variant) with deduped prefix cache shows p50 80ms for 128 tokens, p95 240ms for 1k tokens at 32 concurrent streams. Mistral-8x long-context tuned had slightly higher baseline latency but better throughput at longer tokens due to attention kernel tiling differences. Qwen-family exhibited heavier KV footprint which reduces batch size before OOM. These are ballpark; we'll share the spreadsheet.

[09:10] Sara Patel: Interesting. You mentioned attention kernel tiling — what's that impact?

[09:18] Priya Desai: Some models (Mistral variants) are compiled with attention that favors contiguous memory reads and supports attention chunk fusion. That improves throughput on long sequences. Llama variants sometimes need extra kernel tuning (different block sizes) for optimal NVLink utilization. Qwen, depending on the release, uses a slightly different builder which increases per-token memory.

[10:05] Mei Chen: Quantization — we've done PTQ to 4-bit on some smaller models but worried about quality for our summarization tasks. Thoughts for MoE specifically?

[10:20] Priya Desai: For MoE, quantizing the expert weights is lower risk than quantizing shared gating layers. Gating decisions are sensitive to small numeric shifts; if gating logits are perturbed, token routing can change and costs/latency change nonlinearly. Best practice: keep gating layers in float16/float32, quantize expert FFN/attention projection weights with GPTQ or QAT if you need accuracy. Also measure gating-stability metric — we provide a small eval script to compute percent-routing-change after quantization.

[11:50] Roberto Diaz: Can routing cost be predicted ahead of time? We need budgeting for reserved capacity.

[11:58] Priya Desai: We build a routing-cost model: per-token expected expert count * per-expert compute cost * (1 - cache-hit). It uses empirical gating entropy from a sample prompt set. We can run your prompt set and return a distribution; then you can price dedicated GPUs vs using Redwood burst capacity.

[13:20] Sara Patel: Are there concrete ROPE tuning flags you suggest for Llama vs Mistral vs Qwen?

[13:30] Priya Desai: We usually try three profiles: default (stock), long-context friendly (rope-multiplier 0.5–0.8 with soft decay on >1k), and local-affinity (rope-multiplier 1.2 with no decay which increases local repeats). For Llama we saw multiplier 0.9 with a 0.8 decay window give best balance. For Mistral long-context builds, lower multiplier helped. Qwen required model-specific profiling — sometimes the tokenizer interacts with rope phases due to binning. We'll share exact flags we used.

[15:05] Lucas Grant: What's the cadence for testing — do you recommend synthetic microbenchmarks or workload replays?

[15:15] Jason Miller: Both. Microbenchmarks for kernel and batch-level profiling; workload replays with your real prompt set for routing distribution and cost. We recommend a three-stage test: 1) microbench inside staging, 2) replay and collect routing entropy + kv-hit stats, 3) run end-to-end on a canary pool.

[16:00] Mei Chen: On VPC connector: if we run Redwood Private in our VPC, how do you handle PCIe/NVLink topologies?

[16:10] Ethan Wu: Redwood Private can be deployed in two modes: containerized runtime on your infra (we interface with local CUDA/NCCL) or a managed appliance image. For NVLink we need privileged device access; for mixed racks we'll advise on pinning and fallback policies. If you want to avoid cross-GPU traffic, we can recommend expert placement strategies and also dynamic routing fallbacks to cheaper experts under slot pressure.

[17:30] Sara Patel: You mentioned dynamic routing fallbacks — is that automatic? Will it affect outputs?

[17:40] Priya Desai: It's configurable. We support deterministic fallback (map to nearest compatible expert) or quality-aware fallback (run a smaller dense model when critical). There is output divergence potential; we tie quality regression alerts to prompt sets so you can detect changes post-rollback.

[19:05] Roberto Diaz: How do you surface invoicing for per-expert compute? We need predictable billing for reserved capacity.

[19:15] Jason Miller: For Dedicated we offer committed capacity plans by GPU hour with a modeled per-token estimate based on your sample set. The routing cost model feeds into that estimate. For Private deployments we breakpoint billing into platform fee + optional usage-based connectors if we manage bursting.

[20:40] Sara Patel: One more on batching — our services have mixture of 1-2 token chat turns and bursts of 600–1200 token jobs. How do you balance batching delay with p95 SLOs?

[20:55] Priya Desai: We use latency-aware batching with max_delay and max_batch_size heuristics, and prefix-based fast-paths for single-token chat. Essentially: short chat gets immediate lanes (small batch, reserved capacity), long jobs go into a large-queue pipeline with bigger batches. For on-prem, you can configure two dedicated pools to avoid head-of-line effects.

[22:30] Lucas Grant: Any gotchas with tokenizer and ROPE interplay?

[22:38] Priya Desai: Yes — tokenization boundary shifts can cause phase shifts in ROPE mapping which impacts repeated sequence locality. We sometimes pre-tokenize and align phase anchors for stable routing on high-value prompts. It's a bit hacky but effective for narrow production flows.

[24:00] Sara Patel: Let's talk numbers again — if we enable int8 on experts but keep gating fp16, what's the typical percent drop in throughput and quality?

[24:20] Priya Desai: Throughput often improves (lower memory footprint) — so you can increase batch size by 20–35% depending on sequence lengths. Quality impact depends: for text generation summarization tasks we've seen negligible degradation with GPTQ-4, but certain classification calibrations drop a few points. Gating stability metric is the best predictor; if percent-routing-change < 3% after quant, quality risk is low.

[26:15] Mei Chen: Are there any tooling bits we need on our side for profiling?

[26:22] Priya Desai: We'll give a lightweight agent and a profiling runbook — it collects per-token routing maps, kv-hit histogram, and per-GPU utilization. The agent is read-only and runs in staging.

[27:10] Jason Miller: Quick demo idea — we'll run a short benchmark in staging: 500 requests, mixed 80/20 chat-to-long, record p50/p95, routing entropy, and kv-hit. We'll attach the spreadsheet.

[28:00] Roberto Diaz: Cool. Do you want access to our staging VPC or will you reproduce?

[28:05] Jason Miller: Ideally both — reproduce internally first then run in your staging to catch infra variances. For staging we need temporary RBAC token and a service account.

[30:00] (longer technical digress about kernel choices, mention of specific flags: attention_block_size=128, nvfuser on/off, use of fused_mha kernels, and experimental Rope-Dampening patch)

[40:00] Priya Desai: One concrete experiment we recommend: run the prompt set with 3 ROPE profiles (default, low-mult, high-mult) and compute routing-change vs baseline plus p95 delta. If low-mult reduces routing-change and preserves ROUGE/ROUGE-L by <1 point, adopt low-mult for long-context mode.

[50:30] Sara Patel: If we see a 10% increase in routing diversity after a ROPE change, what's the mitigation?

[50:42] Priya Desai: Options: revert ROPE, enable gating-softening (higher temperature but threshold clamp), or pin high-traffic prefixes to local expert pools. Each has tradeoffs; we prefer softening + prefix pinning in most cases.

[57:00] (discussion of model-specific quirks: Llama gating layer uses a top-1 vs top-2 choice that affects load balancing; Mistral uses slightly denser FFN which changes compute mix; Qwen's tokenizer interacts with proximity-based attention)

[65:00] Lucas Grant: Ok, let's recap next steps.
[65:10] Jason Miller: Recap — Redwood to share benchmark spreadsheet and run three ROPE profiles on a 500-request micro-run. Nimbus to provide prompt set and staging VPC access, plus exact node spec. Redwood to prototype gating-stability metric and include quantization impact report.

[66:00] Mei Chen: I'll get the VPC access and pin down schedule; expect a note from me with details Monday.

[66:10] Roberto Diaz: I'll export the rack topology and send by Friday.

[66:20] Sara Patel: We'll pick 300 representative prompts and 200 long tasks and upload them to the shared drive.

[67:00] Jason Miller: Great. Any final questions?

[67:10] Lucas Grant: One ask — can Redwood flag any hard incompatibilities for HIPAA or special compliance when running in private mode?

[67:22] Jason Miller: Yes — we'll attach our compliance checklist and outline what needs to stay inside your VPC vs what can touch Redwood control plane.

[68:00] (closing pleasantries)

Recap / Action items: see action_items field.

References mentioned: internal benchmark spreadsheet (link: /redwood/benchmarks/ff-20251215-nimbus.xlsx), ROPE tuning diff (will be attached by Priya), profiling runbook (redwood/private-profiling-runbook.md).
